monument_name: Vināyaka Pañcadevala Kālikā Devī Mandira (built in the second half of the 20th cent.)
description_en: Vināyaka Pañcadevala Kālikā Devī Mandira is a small Temple of Goddesses Kālikā built in the second half of the twentieth century on a large complex, surrounded by four mediaevalśikharatemples. The complex is located in Binayak, one of the Achham district's main market towns.The Temple is a single room and faces northeast. Its door is framed by rough-cut stone slab doorjambs that support another, long, rough-cut stone slab serving as a lintel. The ceiling is constructed with roughly cut stones in a corbelled dome technique. The sanctum contains movable stone images of recent origins, as well as a stone block with a rosette carved on it. This element must have come from medievalśikharatemples, most likely ACH0070 or ACH0071. A stone image of an anthropomorphic figure wearing aṭopī(men's traditional hat) and raising both hands in the air leans against the northwestern wall (object number ACH0073-001). This image could not be identified. Similarly, it was not possible to identify which image was considered as Kālikā Devī's.Outside, a cruciform stone block is placed on top of the Temple, which must be a top part of one of the site's two smallestśikharatemples (ACH0070 or ACH0071), given that the latter were partially dismantled until the second half of the twentieth century. Ayajñakuṇḍa(sacrificial pit) made of four small stones stands in front of the Temple. Two stone pillars precede the pit, which is connected by a chain to which a dozen metal bells are attached. The Temple is a more recent creation. There are no inscriptions indicating its construction. Nonetheless, it does not appear on photos taken by Marc Gaborieau in 1968 CE (published in Sharma 1972, Pl. 2), indicating that it was built after that date.The complex of these four temples in Binayak is known as Pañcadevala, which translates as 'five temples'. This emic designation is typically applied to groups of more than two temples, even if when there are more or fewer than five temples. However, Pañcadeval is also a term for five temples built on a quincunx plan, also referred to aspañcāyatana(skt. 'Five altars'). The Pañcadevala plan is mostly found in the districts of Dailekh, Achham and Kalikot, which corresponds to the Rāskoṭi kings' domain (Andolfatto 2019 and Andolfatto 2022). This dynasty ruled from the late fourteenth century to the late eighteenth century.The group of Binayak Pañcadevala has often been considered as a Pañcadevala, without regard for the actual plan. According to Dilli Raj Sharma, '[...] the temples of Vināyak are built to serve the idea of the pañcha dewal style. However, the structural elements do not fit the plan of five temples' (Sharma 2012, p. 228).  According to the general plan, the site only has fourśikharatemples. However, it is unlikely that it was ever built as a Pañcadevala group. The Temple ACH0072 contains an inscription from ŚS 1202 (1280 CE). A temple of comparable size is constructed north-west of the Temple ACH0072. These two temples were most likely constructed at the same time.The two smallerśikharatemples are oriented in a way that has not been seen on any known Pañcadevala of the Karnali basin. Unless we are in presence of an uncomplete and new type of Pañcadevala, theśikharasACH0070 and ACH0071 must be later additions, dating from the late 13th century to the 15th century.The monuments of Binayak are described by Prayag Sharma (Sharma 1972) and the ŚS 1202 inscription of ACH0072 is discussed by Mahes Raj Pant (Pant 2009).
monument_assessment: Good (very few light surface damages, renovated or repaired)

historical_events.event_description: The exact date of construction of the Kālikā Devī Mandira is unknown but it can be situtated in the second half of the 20th century CE. This is indicated by the monument's absence from Marc Gaborieau's 1968 photos. On the other hand, one can make out the temple in a photo published in Dilli Raj Sharma's 2012Heritage of Western Nepal. Art and Architecture(Sharma 2012, p. 226, Pl. 60b.).
